//: BEHAVIOUR CHANGES — what an existing verb now COSTS or REFUSES differently.
Not a changelog. A new verb costs nothing until you reach for it and can be discovered
whenever; an existing verb that starts costing minutes, or refusing where it used to warn,
changes behaviour for people who never asked for anything, in the middle of whatever they were
doing. Only the second kind earns an interruption. If everything lands here the notice becomes
noise and gets ignored exactly when it matters.
This file SHIPS with the payload and is refreshed on every install, so the installed copy is
the record as of your install. `status` compares it against the one on main and names only the
entries you have not seen. No extra stamping, and nothing to keep in sync by hand.
seq is monotonic and never reused — it is the ordering, since commit shas have none.
The test for whether an entry belongs here: would somebody who changed nothing about how they
use game_loop notice this? If no, leave it out.
AN ENTRY SHOULD NAME THE CONSEQUENCE, not only the change. A consumer of this file demonstrated
why: it checked four entries in ten minutes instead of reading 1255 lines of guard, and the one
that mattered most to it was the one whose consequence it had to work out for itself. `change`
says what moved; `consequence` says what somebody might now do WRONG. The second is the reason
anyone reads this file, and it is the half an author is worst placed to notice, because the
author already knows not to make the mistake.
EVERY ENTRY CARRIES EVERY FIELD, and the suite refuses one that does not. Adding `consequence` to
seq 1 alone reproduced the exact defect the field was added to fix: for the other four a consumer
reading `consequence` got nothing, and nothing distinguished 'predates the field' from 'the
author judged there is no consequence'. Two causes, one indistinguishable result, and only the
author holds the difference. If an entry genuinely has no consequence, say so IN the field with a
reason -- an absence must be a decision, not a gap.
`schema` is an integer and consumers should pin to it. This file announces changes to game_loop's
verbs and nothing announced changes to THIS FILE: adding a field is safe, but renaming `change`
or dropping `why_it_qualifies` would break a programmatic reader silently. Bump it when a field
is renamed or removed; adding one does not require a bump.
seq 2 was CORRECTED after a consumer read the entry against the source and found the record
less precise than the code. The entry said English false-positives now run; the source comment
three lines below the fix says the bare verb as a whole word still trips it. Both were written
by the same author in the same commit and both were accurate — the limit was simply written
where a reader of the record never looks. An entry must carry its own caveats, because the
person acting on it is not reading the guard.

changes.change: now re-runs the suite once per stale pattern. Making install.sh, test/run.py and verify.yaml gated files was correct, but a change touching several of them went from roughly one suite run to five — seconds to 2-4 minutes. Run `verify` as its own earlier step; under an autonomy mandate a verb that quietly became slow reads as an idle session.
changes.consequence: an agent that reads a slow verify as HUNG will interrupt it or route around it, and then commits into a tree whose owed checks never recorded a pass — the exact failure the instruction exists to prevent. If you brief agents to run verify, tell them to expect minutes and that it has not hung. Reported by a consumer who found this entry mattered more to it than the one written for it.
changes.why_it_qualifies: the first entry, written before the field existed

changes.change: a configured deploy verb now requires a word boundary on BOTH sides, where it previously had one only before the verb. Calls refused because the verb appeared as a SUBSTRING of ordinary English — 'file surgery' contains 'surge' — now run. NARROWED, NOT REMOVED: the bare verb as a WHOLE WORD in prose still trips it, deliberately. A sentence merely mentioning 'docker push' is still refused, because narrowing to command position would miss a real deploy nested in an interpreter argument, and missing a real publish is the expensive direction.
changes.why_it_qualifies: an existing verb stopped refusing calls it used to refuse
changes.consequence: if you worked around a SUBSTRING false block by rewording, the reword is now unnecessary — but if you reworded prose containing the bare verb as a whole word, YOU STILL NEED IT. Check which kind you had. And if you deleted a verb from deploy_verbs to get past a false block, it is no longer blocked at all: confirm deploy_verbs still lists what you meant.

changes.change: a commit whose TARGET TREE is built from a variable (git -C "$TREE" commit, or a cd through a variable) is now DENIED. It previously passed SILENTLY, because the gate could not read the path and treated unreadable as fine. Nothing about how you commit has to change for this to start blocking you.
changes.why_it_qualifies: silent pass became a denial — the sharpest kind of entry this file is for, and it went unrecorded for weeks while a consumer taught its agents the old behaviour as a measured finding
changes.consequence: an orchestrator committing through `git -C "$TREE"` for weeks, changing nothing, is now BLOCKED. And any brief that told agents a variable-built target passes silently is now false — which is how this was found: a consumer had read the old behaviour correctly, written it down, and could not tell a stale reading from an absent record.

changes.change: an INLINE value over 400 characters is now REFUSED, and must come from the option's --<name>-file twin. A long --notes, --learning or --assert that worked yesterday stops working today. The bound exists because a quoted shell argument is code to the shell first and mangled prose is indistinguishable from short prose.
changes.why_it_qualifies: an existing verb refuses input it used to accept
changes.consequence: a script or an agent that composes a long --notes/--learning/--assert inline fails at the point of the call. In an unattended run that costs the turn, so move composed prose to the --<name>-file twin BEFORE you rely on it rather than after it refuses.

changes.change: a state-changing verb that nobody enumerated now reaches the standing-writes / authorize POLICY instead of failing closed before it. Calls that were refused as unclassifiable — resolve, merge-adjacent review verbs on first-party servers — are now governed by your mcp_writes and mcp_standing_writes settings rather than blocked outright. It does not make them free; it makes them decidable.
changes.why_it_qualifies: an existing verb stopped refusing outright and started deferring to policy, which changes what an unattended run can complete
changes.consequence: if you were relying on unclassifiable-verbs-fail-closed as your safety margin, that margin is now your mcp_writes and mcp_standing_writes settings instead. Read them and confirm they say what you meant; the default is still `gated`, so an unconfigured project is unchanged.

changes.change: a new OPT-IN key, mcp_trusted_servers, permits every call to a named server — irreversible verbs, landing verbs and mutating arguments included. Refusal lines moved in the guard, which is why this entry exists.
changes.consequence: none for anyone who does not set the key. A project with no mcp_trusted_servers is refused exactly what it was refused before, asserted in the suite as its own arm. If you DO set it, read the Configure section: this is the widest door in the tool and status reports it in capitals.
changes.why_it_qualifies: IT DOES NOT — recorded with notice:false because the behaviour gate fired and an omission would be indistinguishable from nobody having decided. The test is whether somebody who changed NOTHING would notice; an opt-in key they have not opted into changes nothing for them.

changes.change: marking a commit that is ALREADY marked at that level no longer dies on `tag already exists`. It reports RE-MARKED, leaves the immutable tag untouched, and re-fires the confidence triggers. The same name over a DIFFERENT commit still refuses, and now names the commit it already records instead of passing through a bare git error.
changes.consequence: a mark whose trigger declined for a TRANSIENT reason can be retried. Observed here: the mark landed, its publish trigger correctly declined because HEAD was not pushed yet, and after pushing there was no way back — the record existed and the publication it exists to cause did not. Recovery meant running the trigger script by hand from a path only its author knows, so consumers stayed on the previous stable in the meantime. If you script `--mark` and relied on a non-zero exit to mean 'already marked', that exit is now 0.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a consumer who changed nothing gets a different exit code and a different action from the same command on the same commit. The triggers firing again is the deliberate part, not a side effect.

changes.change: turn-end can now be REFUSED by something other than the mandate gate. A `stop` key in .game_loop/triggers.json attaches a command to turn-end: a NON-ZERO exit blocks the turn and its stderr goes back to the model. Previously `stop` was not a moment at all, so such a key ran nothing and status called it THERE IS NO SUCH MOMENT. It is bounded in three ways that are part of the contract, not implementation detail: a timeout, an unrunnable command or a crash FAILS OPEN loudly (the turn ends UNCHECKED, which is not a pass); after 3 CONSECUTIVE blocks the attachment STANDS DOWN with a notice and the turn ends, resetting the moment it passes once; and it runs only where turn-end would otherwise be allowed, before any checkpoint/arm/park is consumed. Its default timeout is 10s, not the usual 20, because it runs on every turn-end.
changes.consequence: if you already had a `stop` key in triggers.json it was INERT and is now LIVE — a command that used to run never now runs on every turn-end and can block it. That is the silent-pass-became-a-denial shape, and it is the one group here who changed nothing. For everyone else the moment is opt-in and nothing changes. If you attach one: do not design around the stand-down bound (it is there for the case where your check is RIGHT and the thing it wants is impossible), exit 0 when you cannot tell rather than blocking on an unanswered question, and expect its timeout on every turn you take.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a new way for an existing verb to refuse. An install with no `stop` attachment is byte-identical, but an install that already carried the key gets a live gate it never enabled, and every attachment inherits a bound and a fail-open that decide what happens when its condition cannot be cleared.

changes.change: two exit codes moved. A harness SCRIPT that could not be compared now reports status 'unreadable' at exit 2 — it previously fell through every branch to 'clean' at exit 0, with a detail sentence claiming every script was byte-identical. And 'code-drifted' now exits 1 rather than falling to the default 2: the scripts were read and they differ, which is a determined finding, not an inability to tell.
changes.consequence: if you branch on this verb's exit code you will see trees you were told were clean now reported as undetermined. That is the point: the old answer was wrong. An orchestrator refusing to integrate on drifted-or-undetermined was walked through by a false clean, putting a drifted worktree's branch on trunk. The JSON now carries false_clean_before_fix:true exactly when the old code would have said clean, so a consumer can scan trees and find what was mis-certified — nothing else records it, and it cannot be re-derived after a merge.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a consumer who changed nothing gets different exit codes from the same verb on the same tree, and at least one consumer's merge gate branches on exactly those codes. The behaviour gate did NOT fire — no refusal line matched its regex — so this entry is a judgement rather than a forced one, on the file's own test: would somebody who changed nothing notice?

changes.verb: Write/Edit on the project's rule files
changes.change: the write guard now REFUSES Write/Edit to .game_loop/config.json, INVARIANTS.md and verify.yaml when the file already exists. LEDGER.md is unaffected — it is notes, not policy. Seeding a rule file that does NOT exist is still allowed, which is what keeps installers and worktree provisioning working.
changes.consequence: a session can no longer edit the policy that governs it. If you have anything that rewrites config.json from inside a run — widening mcp_* lists, adding an allow_write_root, adjusting deploy_verbs — it now needs `game_loop authorize --path <the file> --reason "<the human's words>"`, which is single-use and logged. Provisioning that CREATES these files is untouched, deliberately: an orchestrator that provisions worktrees by running install.sh keeps working.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a write that used to succeed now returns permissionDecision deny. It closes the case where a stuck agent widened its own MCP policy to unblock itself and reported the edit as a fix — the rule against that was a sentence in llms.txt, which is INV1's own example of what does not hold.

changes.change: seq 10 denied the RULE files and left config.local.json open. A session could widen its own effective policy through it, because its keys merge with UNION semantics — read_roots, allow_write_roots, deploy_verbs, generated_globs and every mcp_* grant are additive there and cannot be narrowed by the project's own config. It is now denied too, whether or not the file exists. Separately, `worktree --porcelain` now COMPARES config.local.json and reports notes-drifted (exit 3) when both trees carry one and they disagree.
changes.consequence: a session can no longer author the local override; a human editing it, or a layer above writing it into a tree from its own process, never passes through the hook and is unaffected. For the compare: a worktree that simply has no local wiring while its parent does still reports clean — only a real disagreement is drift, and it warns at exit 3 rather than blocking.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a write that succeeded under seq 10 now returns deny, and a tree that certified clean can now report notes-drifted. Found by a consumer who verified seq 10 before depending on it and walked through the second door I had recommended to them for arming a waiting probe.

changes.change: `authorize --reason` now REFUSES a narrow, named class of reason: one citing the agent's own instructions ("brief instructs", "the brief", "my prompt", "task says", "as instructed", and similar). The refusal names the two real routes — ask via `arm`, or report upward if you were dispatched. The record and the log also now carry asked_via_arm, saying whether a question was armed in this session.
changes.consequence: if anything you run authorises from a dispatched brief rather than a human's words, it now fails instead of recording. A human's actual sentence still authorises unchanged — only self-citation is refused, and a human who happens to say "the brief says to" loses a rephrase. asked_via_arm does not gate anything; it makes a hatch spent with nobody asked readable as different from one spent after asking.
changes.why_it_qualifies: an authorize call that succeeded before now returns non-zero. It closes a case observed in the wild: an unattended Crawler spent the human's hatch twice on its own brief, and the log then read as human-sanctioned when nobody had been asked — which destroys the property single-use-and-logged exists for.

changes.verb: the commit gate, on a tree with no harness
changes.change: the refusal now prints a PASTEABLE install command for the exact unharnessed tree, and records itself in the PARENT's log as kind commit_gate_unharnessed_tree. The refusal itself is unchanged in what it refuses.
changes.consequence: if you grep your log for how often this gate fires, you will now find entries where before there were none — the commit tree has no .game_loop/ and therefore no log of its own, so every one of these was previously invisible in the only place a reviewer would look. Nothing is refused that was permitted before.
changes.why_it_qualifies: a consumer who changed nothing sees different refusal text and new log lines. Reported after four --no-verify commits in one day: the honest remedies were a manual step and an impossibility, so the escape hatch won every time and left no trace of the gate that prompted it. The behaviour gate did NOT fire — no refusal line matched its regex — so this entry is a judgement.
